# Healthcare Domain: Data Pitfalls

**Page type:** detail page (one h2 per pitfall, each followed by a two-column obj-table row: text left 50%, canvas right 50%)
**HTML title tag:** Healthcare Domain - Data Pitfalls

**Subtitle:** EHR data is generated by care delivery, not research protocols — informative missingness, coding noise, and time biases distort every naive analysis.

## Missing Data Means Healthy (Informative Missingness)

**Tested-Only Glucose Averages 142 mg/dL, the Population ~100**

- Lab tests are ordered when clinicians suspect illness, creating selection bias in observed values
- Patients with missing lab values are systematically healthier than those with recorded values
- Imputing missing values with population means or medians biases toward sicker patients
- EHR data is generated by care delivery, not research protocols - missingness is never random
- A "normal" creatinine in the database is still from someone sick enough to be tested

**Example:** In a hospital database, average recorded blood glucose is 142 mg/dL. But this only includes patients whose doctors ordered the test. The true population average is ~100 mg/dL. Building a diabetes risk model on observed-only data dramatically overestimates baseline risk.

### Visualization (canvas `canvas1`, 720×240)

Two overlaid Gaussian density curves: true population vs tested-only distribution of blood glucose.

- **Title (bold 17px, `#1a5276`):** "Lab Value Distribution: Tested vs All Patients".
- **All Patients curve (green):** Gaussian mean 100, sd 20, amplitude 140; fill `rgba(39,174,96,0.3)`, stroke `#27ae60` width 2.
- **Tested Patients curve (red, shifted right):** Gaussian mean 142, sd 25, amplitude 110; fill `rgba(231,76,60,0.3)`, stroke `#e74c3c` width 2.
- **X axis:** dark `#2c3e50` baseline with tick labels 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 and axis title "Blood Glucose (mg/dL)".
- **Legend (13px, top left):** green "All Patients (true distribution)"; red "Tested Patients Only (observed in EHR)".
- **Annotation:** dashed purple `#8e44ad` (dash 4/3, width 1.5) horizontal arrow from x=100 to x=142 labeled "Selection bias gap" in 11px purple.

## Sub-Population Reference Ranges

**One Range Flags 40% of Healthy Patients as Abnormal**

- Normal lab ranges vary significantly by age, sex, ethnicity, and altitude of residence
- A single "normal range" misclassifies healthy individuals from different demographics
- Hemoglobin: males 13.5-17.5, females 12.0-16.0, high-altitude residents +1-2 g/dL
- Creatinine "normal" for a muscular 25-year-old male is "abnormal" for an 80-year-old female
- Pediatric ranges differ dramatically from adult ranges and change with development

**Example:** An ML model flags 40% of healthy African American patients as having abnormal eGFR because it uses a single reference range. Race-adjusted formulas (now controversial) were introduced to address this but created their own biases in kidney transplant eligibility.

## Immortal Time Bias

**Patients Must Survive to Get the Drug — 45% "Benefit" Is Artifact**

- Time between cohort entry and treatment start is "immortal" - patient must survive to receive treatment
- Attributing immortal time to the treatment group artificially inflates survival estimates
- Common in observational studies of drug effectiveness from EHR data
- Can create apparent 30-50% survival benefits that are entirely artifactual
- Landmark analysis or time-varying covariates are proper fixes

**Example:** A study finds statin users have 45% lower cancer mortality. But "statin user" is defined as anyone who filled a prescription during follow-up. Patients had to survive long enough to get the prescription - the immortal time is misclassified as "protected" time.

- **Title (bold 17px, `#1a5276`):** "Immortal Time Bias: Treatment Timeline".
- **Patient A (Treated), timeline at y=75:** gray `#bdc3c7` line from "Cohort entry" dot (dark `#2c3e50`, labeled) to death. Green band `rgba(39,174,96,0.3)` from entry to Rx start (40% of timeline) labeled in green: "IMMORTAL TIME" / "(must survive to get Rx)". Red `#e74c3c` 6px dot labeled "Rx Start" at the 40% mark. Blue band `rgba(41,128,185,0.3)` from Rx start toward the end. "X" death marker labeled "Death" near the right end.
- **Patient B (Untreated), timeline at y=150:** short gray line from "Cohort entry" dot ending at 25% of the timeline with an "X" marker; red 10px annotations: "Death (before Rx possible)" and "Classified as \"untreated\" = bias!".
- **Time axis labels (11px `#7f8c8d`, bottom):** "Month 0", "Month 6" (at 40%), "Month 12" (right end).

## Diagnosis Code Noise (ICD Coding Errors)

**Hospital A Codes 60% More Sepsis Than B, Same Patients**

- ICD-10 has 72,000+ codes; coders choose under time pressure with incomplete information
- Same condition can map to multiple codes (e.g., diabetes has 100+ ICD-10 codes)
- Estimated 15-30% of diagnosis codes have meaningful errors or imprecision
- "Rule-out" diagnoses are often coded the same as confirmed diagnoses
- Coding practices vary by institution, payer, and financial incentives (upcoding)

**Example:** A sepsis prediction model trained at Hospital A (which codes aggressively for billing) shows 60% higher sepsis prevalence than Hospital B. The difference is not in patient populations but in coding practices. The model fails catastrophically when deployed at Hospital B.

  - E11.8 (15%) — "With unspecified comp." at (360, 155)

## Small n, Many Features (p >> n)

**50 Patients, 20,000 Genes — 95% CV Accuracy Replicates at 52%**

- Genomics/proteomics studies: 50-200 patients, 20,000+ features per patient
- Any ML model can achieve perfect training accuracy by memorizing - overfitting is guaranteed
- Standard cross-validation still overfits when feature selection is done before splitting
- Published gene signatures rarely replicate: ~85% fail independent validation
- Multiple testing correction (Bonferroni) is too conservative; FDR methods essential

**Example:** A cancer genomics study with 50 patients and 20,000 genes reports a 30-gene signature with 95% accuracy (CV). An independent lab with 200 new patients finds accuracy is 52% - no better than a coin flip. The original result was pure overfitting.

### Visualization (canvas `canvas5`, 720×240)

Composite: patient-dot grid, dense feature-matrix strip, and diverging train/test accuracy curves.

- **Title (bold 17px, `#1a5276`):** "p >> n: Overfitting Guaranteed".
- **Patient grid (top left, labeled "n = 50 patients"):** 50 blue `#3498db` dots in a 10×5 grid (6px dots, 10px spacing).
- **Feature matrix (top right, labeled "p = 20,000 features (genes)"):** 5×80 strip of small red cells at random opacity `rgba(231,76,60, rand·0.7+0.1)`, 4×10px each, with gray note "... 20,000 columns".
- **Accuracy curves (bottom, labeled "Model Accuracy", x-axis "# Features used →"):**
  - Training (green `#27ae60`, width 2.5) through points (x offset, accuracy): `[[0,55],[50,70],[100,82],[200,92],[350,97],[500,99]]` — labeled "Training: 95%+ (memorized)".
  - Test (red `#e74c3c`, width 2.5) through `[[0,55],[50,62],[100,58],[200,54],[350,52],[500,50]]` — labeled "Test: ~50% (coin flip)".

## Lead Time Bias

**Diagnosed 8 Years Earlier → Survival 70% to 99%, Deaths Unchanged**

- Earlier detection appears to improve survival even if treatment has zero effect on death date
- Screening programs can show "improved survival" purely through earlier diagnosis
- 5-year survival rates are systematically misleading for cancers detected by screening
- Only mortality rate (deaths per population) avoids lead time bias; survival time does not
- Overdiagnosis compounds the problem: finding "cancers" that would never cause symptoms

**Example:** Prostate cancer screening shows "5-year survival" went from 70% to 99% after PSA testing was introduced. But overall mortality barely changed. Men were simply diagnosed 8 years earlier on average, making them appear to "survive longer" while dying on the same date.

### Visualization (canvas `canvas6`, 720×240)

Two patient timelines with identical death dates but different measured survival.

- **Title (bold 17px, `#1a5276`):** "Lead Time Bias: Same Death Date, Different \"Survival\"".
- **Without Screening timeline (y=80):** gray `#bdc3c7` line; orange `#e67e22` 6px dot at 55% labeled "Symptoms → Diagnosis"; blue band `rgba(52,152,219,0.3)` from diagnosis to death labeled in blue `#2980b9` "Survival = 3 years"; "X" death marker labeled "Death" near the right end.
- **With Screening timeline (y=160):** green `#27ae60` 6px dot at 15% labeled "Screen → Diagnosis"; light green band `rgba(39,174,96,0.15)` with dashed green outline (dash 3/3) from early detection to the symptom point, labeled in green "LEAD TIME (not extra life)"; blue band `rgba(52,152,219,0.3)` from early detection to death labeled "Apparent Survival = 8 years"; "X" at the same position labeled "Same death date!".
- **Bottom annotation (bold 12px red):** "Same outcome, different measured \"survival\"".

## Regeneration instructions

- **Layout:** h1 + `.subtitle`, then per pitfall an `<h2>` heading (1.4em `#1a5276` with 2px `#2980b9` bottom border) followed by a single-row `.obj-table`: left `<td>` (40%) holds `.obj-title` (a refined restatement of the pitfall name, never a copy of it) + bullet list + `.example` callout, right `<td>` (60%, centered) holds the canvas. Even table rows get background `#fafcfe`.
- **Callouts:** `.example` — background `#f0f4f8`, left border `3px solid #2980b9`, padding 10px 14px, 0.9em, with bold "Example:" lead-in. (A `.philosophy` style — background `#f0f4f8`, left border `4px solid #2980b9`, padding 12px 16px, 0.9em — is defined but unused.)
- **Page style:** body system sans-serif, white background, text `#2a2a2a`, padding 20px 10px, line-height 1.6; h1 1.8em `#1a5276`; subtitle `#666` 1.05em; ul 0.9em `#333`; table cell borders `1px solid #e0e0e0`, padding 20px 24px; `.obj-title` 1.05em weight 600 `#1a5276`; `strong` in `#1a5276`. No nav bar, no back/home links.
- **Canvas:** all canvases 720×240 intrinsic; scale by `window.devicePixelRatio` (cap display at the logical width via `style.maxWidth`, backing store = rendered width × dpr, `ctx.scale` back to logical coordinates) via a shared `setupCanvas(id)` helper. Chart fonts use `-apple-system, sans-serif`.
- **Palette:** primary blue `#1a5276`, secondary blue `#2980b9`/`#3498db`, green `#27ae60`, red `#e74c3c`, orange `#e67e22`/`#f39c12`, purple `#8e44ad`, dark slate `#2c3e50`, gray `#7f8c8d`/`#bdc3c7`.
